newsitem.title: JAPAN: SWIMMING-THORPE THE TALKING POINT OF PAN PACIFICS.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-THORPE THE TALKING POINT OF PAN PACIFICS.

text.p: The swimmer all the other swimmers were talking about at the Pan Pacific Championships didn't set any world records or even win any gold medals.
Instead, 14-year-old Australian Ian Thorpe left world and Olympic champions shaking their heads in disbelief at his times in the major international meet which ended on Wednesday.
"He's pretty impressive. I was his age when he was born," said 28-year-old American Jon Olsen, a double gold medalist at the Atlanta Olympics.
Thorpe, called "Thorpedo" by the Australian media, sent a murmur through the stands on Tuesday when he finished behind 17-year-old teammate Grant Hackett in the men's 400 metres freestyle final.

Hackett swam a great race to win in three minutes 47.27 seconds, the ninth-fastest time ever and the fastest this year, but said he was also stunned by the performance of Thorpe, who finished in 4:49.64.

"I'm young, but he's amazing," Hackett said. Even more amazed was American veteran Chad Carvin, 23, who had no response when Thorpe blasted past him late on the final lap. "The young guns took me to school," said Carvin, who won the same event at the U.S. national championships last month.
Thorpe was tagged with the "Thorpedo" nickname after he started demolishing age-group records in Australia.
He is also the youngest male to ever make an Australian team, beating by one month John Konrads, who made Australia's 1956 Olympic team at 14 years, six months.
Konrads went on to win Olympic gold in 1960 and set half a dozen world records.
Thorpe's 400 metre time in Fukuoka was not even his best. He has posted a 3:53.44, which would have given him eighth spot in the finals at the Atlanta Games last year.
Thorpe's coach Doug Frost said he was looking forward to the Olympics in 2000, which will be held in Thorpe's hometown of Sydney. "We're excited about that. It's where his goals are," Frost said.
